theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon
notes: Watkins's Basic Formula *(é)gʷʰent ógʷʰim. Past of the root present (Ved. imperfect áhan, Av. janat̰, Hitt. preterite kuenta); Greek has the reduplicated aorist (κατ)έπεφνε of the same root and ὄφις in Pindar (not in the local Homer corpus; Il. 6.183 is Bellerophon slaying the Chimaera). The engine prints the augmentless form, which Watkins allows. Verb-initial order follows Vedic and Avestan; Hittite is verb-final. Hittite illuyanka- is not a cognate of *h₁ógʷʰis. Round 2: the two Greek refs are support only (ὄφις and κατέπεφνε come from different passages; review P2); the line stands on Vedic, Avestan and Hittite.

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon
notes: The relative-clause definition of the god or hero by his slaying (Watkins 1995 ch. 37 on Y. 9.8, Yt. 19.40 and the RV 2.12 refrain): subject relative *yo- + past of *gʷʰen- in three branches: Av. yō janat̰ ažīm (Y. 9.8), Ved. yó áhim jaghā́na (RV 2.12.11), Gk Ζεύς, ὅς μιν κατέπεφνε 'Zeus, who slew him' (Od. 5.128, of Iasion). Round 2: the round-1 Greek locus Il. 24.758 was an object relative ('whom Apollo slew') and is replaced by the subject relative of Od. 5.128 (checked in the local Homer). The copular main clause is dropped (RV 2.12 has a noun predicate, sá ... índraḥ, which has no lexeme). *h₁ógʷʰis is Indo-Iranian only here (the Greek object is a man), so it is interpolated; the relative *yo- (Ved. yá-, Av. ya-, Gk ὅς) is cognate in all three but is closed-class, which the builder does not credit. Tense: Vedic perfect, Avestan imperfect, Greek reduplicated aorist: the past of the root present is chosen as in the Basic Formula. All three loci checked locally.

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon
notes: Second lexical variant of the formula, *terh₂- 'overcome' (Watkins ch. 34), here with the monster as subject (the serpent's first, temporary victory over the Storm God). Hittite tarḫu- is a u-stem present, matching the lexeme térh₂uti; the Vedic counterpart is the negated aorist (Vṛtra 'did not withstand' Indra's weapons), so the two branches agree on root and roles but not on polarity. The serpent is interpolated (Hitt. illuyanka- is not cognate; the Vedic subject is Vṛtra, called áhi- in 1.32.5). Clause-initial nu is Hittite nu=za.

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon
notes: The *terh₂- formula in the other direction: the Storm God 'began to overcome' the serpent (Hittite periphrasis with dai-, rendered as a simple past); Vedic tū́rvasi and Avestan tauruuaiia- show the same u-extended root as Hittite tarḫu-. The object 'serpent' is interpolated (Hitt. illuyanka-, Ved. vṛtrá- are not cognates of *h₁ógʷʰis).

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: Let them overcome him, let them thrust at him, and let them put him at their own feet.

notes: Watkins ch. 33: the Luvian imprecation 'may the gods crush him like reeds, smash him, put him under their feet' (*terh₂-, *wedʰ(h₁)-, *ped-, *dʰeh₁-) against RV 1.32.6-8 (nā́tārīd ... vadhā́nām; like a split reed; at the feet lay the serpent). Reduplicated present for Luvian tatarḫ- (cf. Ved. titar-); imperative 3pl matches Luvian -ndu. The *wedʰh₁- lexeme is glossed 'push, thrust' (LIV), so the English says 'thrust'; Vedic vadh- means 'smite'. The reed simile (*nedo-) and 'under' (Luv. annan) are left out: no usable lexemes. dʰeh₁- 'put' is Luvian only; 'their own' (swos) is interpolated.

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon
notes: Watkins ch. 53 (SLAY ... LIE): the slain adversary lies. *ḱey- 'lie' (Ved. śáye, Av. sōire, Gk. κεῖμαι) and the verbal adjective *gʷʰn̥tó- (Av. jata-, Gk. -φατος in πρόσφατος 'newly slain'; Ved. hatá- in RV 10.108.4). The Greek passage is Hekabe over Hector, not a monster; *h₁ógʷʰis is Vedic only here. Round 2: locus corrected to Il. 24.757–758 (πρόσφατος ends 757, κεῖσαι opens 758; checked).

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: He slew the serpent lying there.

notes: RV 2.12.11 'who slew the serpent, the Dānu, lying (there)': accusative *h₁ógʷʰim with the middle participle *ḱéymh₁nom, exactly Ved. áhiṃ ... śáyānam = Gk. ὄφιν κείμενον (Il. 12.208, the snake dropped by the eagle, lying amid the Trojans). The Greek snake is a portent, not a slain dragon; Greek *gʷʰen- is cited from the Chimaera episode (Il. 6.183). Vedic has the perfect jaghā́na; the past of the root present is chosen as in the Basic Formula.

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: Now the serpent lies; it sleeps.

notes: Watkins 1995 ch. 54 (LIE ... SLEEP, after S. Jamison): the dragon 'lies, sleeps' (Beowulf 2746–2747 in the local Harrison–Sharp text, Watkins' 2745–2746: nū se wyrm ligeð, swefeð). Round 2: the Vedic parallel is now RV 4.19.3, where the serpent is 'sleeping' (suṣupāṇá-, perfect middle participle of intransitive svap-) and 'lying' (āśáyāna-) when Indra strikes it: the plain *swep- 'sleep' of OE swefan, not the causative siṣvapaḥ of RV 1.121.11 used in round 1 (which also duplicated death-otherworld-005). The match is still root-level in formation (Ved. perfect participle, OE thematic present *swépeti). 'Lie' is *legʰ- in Old English but *ḱey- in Vedic: *ḱey- follows the Vedic and is not secure. The serpent is interpolated (OE wyrm < *wr̥mis, Ved. áhi-). RV 1.103.7 (sasántam ... áhim 'the sleeping serpent', Watkins' Vedic example) is support: sas- is another root (*ses-). nu = OE nū (Ved. nú is not in these verses), closed class. All loci checked locally.

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: He bound the serpent with a rope.

notes: The adversary bound with a rope: Ḫupašiya binds the serpent išḫimanta 'with a cord' (Illuyanka, KUB 17.5 i 15′, checked); Satan lies in hell sīmon gesǣled 'bound with ropes' (Genesis B; checked in the local Grein edition, l. 766). Secure is the rope noun *sh₂imṓ: Hitt. išḫiman- = OE sīma (Watkins 1995 ch. 46: *sh₂i-mon-, accent on the suffix). The verb is not shared: Hittite kaleliya- is not cognate and OE sǣlan is a denominative of sāl 'rope' (root *sh₂ey-), so the nasal present *sinéh₂- (Ved. sinā́ti) is interpolated and only root-level. Round 2: Greek ἱμάσσω (Il. 2.782, Zeus lashing the earth around Typhoeus; Watkins' 'phonetic echo' of the Hittite, a denominative of ἱμάς, another formation; round 1's 'Il. 8.543' is really Il. 8.544, horses tied with thongs, and is dropped) and RV 7.84.2 (Varuṇa's bonds, explicitly 'without ropes') are support only; the Genesis locus is now the local edition's. The serpent is interpolated (Hitt. illuyanka- is not cognate; the OE adversary is Satan).

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: You became the striker of the serpent.

notes: Watkins ch. 43: Germanic 'become the bane' (ON at bana verða, OE tō banan weorðan) as the periphrastic continuant of *gʷʰen-, with the agent noun *gʷʰonós = Ved. ghaná- 'striker'; Vedic has the same construction, 'you became the striker of the vṛtras' (RV 1.4.8, cf. 8.96.18). Grípisspá 11: Sigurðr will slay the serpent Fáfnir. 'Become' is *bʰuH- with the Vedic (Gmc. verða is *wert-, Gk. γένοντο *ǵenh₁-), so not secure. Greek φόνος is the action noun (lexeme gʷʰónos-2), not this agent noun. 'Serpent' is interpolated (Ved. vṛtrá-, ON ormr < *wr̥mis). Round 2: Od. 21.24 φόνος is support only (the action noun, not the agent noun). The Germanic n-stem *banô (*gʷʰon-on-) beside Ved. ghaná- (*gʷʰonó-) is a formation-level match. Grípisspá 11 (orm ... at bana verða ... Fáfni), Beowulf 587 (tō banan wurde) and RV 1.4.8 checked locally.

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: He who slays, him they do not slay.

notes: Round 2, rebuilt on the 'slayer not slain' variant of Watkins 1995 ch. 31, which he compares across branches himself: RV 8.84.9 nákir yáṃ ghnánti hánti yáḥ 'whom none slay, who slays' ('like the Old Irish variant above, this is the slayer not slain') and OIr gonait 7 ní genaiter 'they slay and are not slain' (Togail Bruidne Da Derga 783; not in the local corpora). *gʷʰen- stands in both clauses in both branches, the second negated. The round-1 line ('he who slays is slain') was Celtic only: OIr gonas géntar and Welsh wanei wanwyd are now support, as is Il. 18.309 (the figure with κτείνω, lexical replacement per Watkins) and the late Vedic nāyaṃ hanti na hanyate (Kaṭha Up. 1.2.19, checked in the local DCS). The second clause follows the Vedic 3pl active ghnánti (*gʷʰn̥énti); Old Irish has a passive. Order and the correlative so- are interpolated (Vedic has two relative clauses under kṣéti 'he dwells'). RV 8.84.9 checked locally. The relative *yo- is shared but closed-class.

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: With the striker I slay the serpent.

notes: The Basic Formula as performative charm, 1st person present (Watkins ch. 56): Atharvavedic 'with the striker I slay' (in a charm against snakes, the object a real snake: Watkins) and the Old Irish worm charm 'I slay the creature' (gono míl). Shared: *gʷʰen- 1sg present (Ved. hanmi, OIr gono). The instrument ghaná- (*gʷʰonós) and the snake object are Vedic only (AV 10.4.9 checked in the local DCS: ghanena hanmi ... ahiṃ) (OIr míl 'animal' has no usable lexeme).

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: He slew the serpent, and the gods were with him.

notes: HERO SLAY SERPENT with COMPANION (Watkins ch. 36): the Storm God slew the serpent 'and the gods were with him' (Hittite), Indra slew the serpent 'accompanied by Viṣṇu' (Vedic), Bellerophon slew the Chimaera trusting the gods' portents (Greek). Secure is *gʷʰen- only. Hittite DINGIRMEŠ (read šiuneš < *dyew-) is a logogram, so *deywós is interpolated; Hitt. ešer 'they were' (*h₁és-) is Hittite only; ḱóm 'with, beside' stands for katti=šši 'with him' (not cognate). Round 2: the Greek (Bellerophon trusting the gods' portents) is support only: it shares the verb but not the companion clause.

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: The serpent had three heads and six eyes.

notes: Watkins ch. 48: THREE-HEADED and SIX-EYED (Av. Aži Dahāka, Ved. Viśvarūpa). The Greek is the three-headed serpent on Agamemnon's shield-strap, with the dative-of-possession construction κεφαλαὶ δέ οἱ ἦσαν τρεῖς that the PIE line uses. Only 'three' is secure (Ved. tri-, Av. θri-, Gk. τρεῖς); 'head' differs (Ved. śīrṣán- < *ḱr̥h₂s-, Gk. κεφαλή), 'six' and 'eye' are Indo-Iranian only, the copula is Greek only, and *h₁ógʷʰis is Indo-Iranian only (Gk. δράκων).

theme: Storm and Stream: The Water Dragon

plan.english: The serpent devoured horses and men.

notes: Kərəsāspa's serpent Aži Sruuara, 'horse-devouring, man-devouring' (Y. 9.11 = Yt. 19.40; Watkins ch. 56 on the man-slaying beast); the Homeric snake 'that has devoured' poisonous herbs (Il. 22.93-94). Shared is the root *gʷerh₃- 'devour' (Av. -gar-, Gk. βι-βρώ-σκω). The Avestan compounds become a finite clause with plural objects; horses and men are Avestan only (Ved. gohā́ nṛhā́ in RV 7.56.17 has 'cow' and *gʷʰen-), and *h₁ógʷʰis is Avestan only.

plan.english: Let me slay him in vengeance.

notes: Round 3 draft (docs/audits/tier2-round3-drafts.md), from the formula witness scan (docs/research/formula-witness-scan.md); not yet reviewed. Watkins 1995, slaying and vengeance (*gʷʰen- + *kʷoynéh₂; slay-and-avenge-gwhen-kwei). The scan's Celtic witness (OIr guin ~ cin) rests on a disputed etymology of cin and is not used; this line uses an Avestan witness the scan missed. Avestan Rām Yašt (Yt. 15; CAB YtWay8.3d–f): Kərəsāspa asks Vayu yat̰ kaēna nijasāni azəm brāϑrō uruuāxšiia, yat̰ janāni hitāspəm 'that I may come to vengeance for my brother Urvāxšaya, that I may slay Hitāspa'. kaēnā- 'vengeance' = Gk ποινή (*kʷoynéh₂, exact in both); janāni is the present subjunctive 1sg of jan- (*gʷʰénoh₂-), the line's form. Greek Il. 9.632–633 κασιγνήτοιο φονῆος ποινήν … ἐδέξατο 'accepted the blood-price for the killing of a brother' (AGDT attaches φονῆος to ποινήν): ποινή exact, *gʷʰen- only in the derivative φονεύς (root level). So the verb is attested only in Avestan; Greek gives the root. Both passages concern a slain brother (brātar- and κασίγνητος are not cognate). Support Il. 15.116 τίσασθαι φόνον 'to avenge the killing' (τίνω, *kʷey-). Interpolated: the object 'him' (Avestan names Hitāspa) and the instrumental construal 'in vengeance', which joins the two Avestan clauses into one.
